memory_leads.lead: A vessel's registered owner, economic or beneficial owner, parent group and day-to-day operator can be different entities. Historical replay should therefore avoid treating a single company label as the complete ownership-and-control state.

Single-vessel or small-fleet special-purpose owning companies can separate legal title to an asset from group-level strategy, financing, management and economic exposure. Exact company trees require Evidence, but the structural role is important for claims, finance and asset-transfer analysis.

Flag or vessel registry is an asset identity and regulatory interface rather than proof of commercial ownership. Registration connects the vessel to a nationality/administration framework, while economic ownership, technical management and charter control may sit elsewhere.

Bareboat or demise-type charter control can shift possession and operating responsibilities without transferring registered title. This creates a role state in which the party controlling crewing and operation may differ from the legal owner.

Technical management, commercial management and crewing management can be split across different organizations. Maintenance/class compliance, chartering/employment and personnel functions therefore should not be inferred from vessel ownership alone.

Ship management can be performed in-house or outsourced. The management appointment itself is a time-varying relationship whose start, termination and transfer can matter for safety culture, procurement, maintenance, crewing and operating-cost history.

Mortgage recordation and vessel title are linked but distinct from broader borrower or group financing. A vessel can carry registered security while debt economics, guarantees or lender exposure extend beyond the ship-owning entity.

A vessel sale is a multi-state transition rather than a single price event: agreement, conditions/due diligence, financing or mortgage-release preparation, closing, physical/legal delivery, registry/flag transition, management/crew transition and post-delivery operation can occur at different times.

Sale-and-purchase delivery can change ownership while some operational relationships persist temporarily, or change management/flag/insurance simultaneously. Replay therefore needs separate effective times for title/economic exposure and operational control where supportable.

Changes of flag, registry, name, manager, operator or owning SPV can occur without the physical vessel becoming a new asset. Stable vessel identity should therefore be distinguishable from mutable corporate and registry attributes.

Beneficial or economic-control questions are especially important when screening counterparty, financing, sanctions/compliance, claims or related-party exposure, but exact beneficial-ownership conclusions require authoritative current or historical Evidence and should not be guessed from model memory.

Ownership and management transitions can affect continuity of records and counterparties. Charterers, lenders, insurers, class/flag interfaces, suppliers, crews and port agents may need to recognize a new responsible entity even when the vessel's physical employment barely changes.

Known-time can differ from effective ownership/control time. A sale, management transfer or ownership restructuring may be negotiated privately before public or counterparty visibility, so historical replay should not backfill later-known group identity into earlier decisions.

P045 arrest/mortgage memory is refined because a claim against a vessel-owning entity, a group company, an operator or a bareboat charterer may have different operational implications; exact legal reach remains Evidence-only.

P044 insurance memory is refined because policyholder/member, registered owner, manager and economic owner need not be identical roles; blind Memory should not infer coverage or membership from asset ownership.

Atlas counterparty-risk analysis is refined by separating vessel identity from company identity so historical mergers, bankruptcies, fleet sales and restructurings do not accidentally erase the continuing life of the physical ship.

Atlas capital-cycle analysis is refined because secondhand asset transfers can move vessels between owners and financing structures without changing total fleet supply, while changing leverage, cost base and strategic behavior.
The atlas already records broad ownership transfers and capital-provider changes in downturns; P046 adds role and identity separation rather than repeating that ships change hands.
Generic temporal precision, provenance and Memory-not-Evidence rules are already Baseline semantics; P046 applies them to vessel identity, title, management and control changes.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Registry and title rules are jurisdiction-specific and require dated authoritative Evidence.
Entity identity and control are claim-specific historical/current facts requiring corporate, registry, contractual or other authoritative Evidence.
Provider and current-market rankings are directory/current-state claims outside blind Memory.
Transaction documents and exact closing mechanics vary by deal and law; blind Memory retains only structural lifecycle states.

stop_reason: The vessel identity/control layer is populated across registered/economic ownership, SPV/group, flag/registry, bareboat control, technical/commercial/crewing management, mortgage recordation and sale/delivery transitions. Further recall becomes registry-, title-, beneficial-owner-, transaction-, company- or jurisdiction-specific.
truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation; no vessel ownership, beneficial ownership, control, registry status, flag, mortgage recordation, management appointment, sale/delivery, company relationship or jurisdiction-specific title rule is verified.
